title: Only the U.S. Senate can prevent the next FTX
gist: An a16z crypto policy argument that the Senate's September 15 procedural vote on the Digital Asset Market Clarity (CLARITY) Act is the decisive moment for U.S. digital asset market structure: the bill would extend century-old custody, segregation, disclosure and insider-selling rules to spot crypto intermediaries, settle SEC/CFTC jurisdiction with a statutory control test, and bar passive stablecoin yield. The piece frames the status quo as the real 'Wild West' and argues agency rulemaking cannot substitute for statute, with stablecoin supply past $300 billion and tokenized assets past $30 billion raising the cost of inaction.

insights.claim: The Senate votes on September 15, 2026 on whether to open debate on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, the bill's first shot on the Senate floor after the Banking and Agriculture Committees cleared their versions earlier in the year.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: A binary, dated catalyst for U.S.-listed crypto exchanges, custodians and token issuers — the cloture outcome is the near-term signal to trade around.
insights.quote: Tomorrow, on September 15, the Senate votes on whether to open debate.
insights.locator: Tomorrow, on September 15, the Senate votes

insights.claim: The House has already passed crypto market structure legislation twice, most recently in July 2025 by a bipartisan 294-134 vote, meaning the Senate is the only remaining bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: A wide bipartisan House margin implies that if the Senate clears procedure, final passage probability rises sharply — the risk is concentrated in one chamber.
insights.locator: Congress has been trying for years

insights.claim: Any version of the bill that reaches the President will be a compromise in which the crypto industry accepts entry into the U.S. regulatory perimeter in exchange for a statutory foundation and clear rules.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Signals the industry's largest policy backer is pre-committing to concessions — expect the final text to be more restrictive than the House version, and price compliance costs accordingly.
insights.locator: Should a version of CLARITY reach the President

themes.theme: FTX post-mortem: absence of ordinary safeguards, not sophistication

insights.claim: FTX did not collapse because of a sophisticated scheme but because there were no independent custodian, segregated asset, or disclosure requirements, and no regulatory oversight enforcing them; the fraud surfaced as an $8 billion hole when customers tried to withdraw.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Reframes crypto blowup risk as a custody-and-segregation question, so due diligence should focus on independent custody and proof of segregation rather than on exchange sophistication.
insights.quote: FTX simply hid that they misappropriated customer assets, because there were no independent custodian, segregated assets, or disclosure requirements.
insights.locator: FTX did not fail because regulators missed

insights.claim: The relevant safeguards have existed for nearly a century — customer property segregation for futures commission merchants under the Commodity Exchange Act of 1936, the SEC's Customer Protection Rule for broker-dealers, and the Securities Investor Protection Act of 1970 — but simply do not extend to spot digital asset markets.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Defines the exact compliance template spot venues will have to build toward — custody, reserve, capital, disclosure and examination infrastructure vendors are the direct beneficiaries.
insights.locator: The safeguards that could have prevented this

insights.claim: The absence of a clear rulebook let an offshore exchange with no meaningful disclosure obligations compete directly against domestic firms navigating a patchwork of state requirements and shifting enforcement, effectively penalizing compliant behavior.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: If passed, the regulatory arbitrage advantage of offshore venues narrows — a relative margin and market-share tailwind for compliant U.S. intermediaries.
insights.quote: That is not a market. That is a penalty on good behavior.
insights.locator: The absence of a clear rulebook is also

insights.claim: Nearly four years after the bankruptcy, creditors have recovered close to $10 billion and the Justice Department secured a conviction for misappropriating customer funds, but Congress has still not established preventive safeguards.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Enforcement-after-the-fact has been the only U.S. response so far; assume tail risk in unregulated venues remains unchanged until statute passes.
insights.locator: Nearly four years have passed since FTX

themes.theme: What the CLARITY Act actually changes

insights.claim: The CLARITY Act would bring digital commodity brokers, dealers and exchanges inside the regulatory perimeter with segregation of customer property, qualified custody, affiliate conflict restrictions, mandatory disclosure, listing standards, limits on insider selling, and a named compliance officer personally answerable for the firm's adherence to law.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist of new operating costs and moats: firms already running qualified custody and listing standards gain, thinly-capitalized venues face consolidation pressure.
insights.locator: The CLARITY Act brings digital commodity brokers

insights.claim: The bill would replace a project's unfalsifiable claim to be 'sufficiently decentralized' with a statutory test based on control.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: A control-based test is objectively testable, so token cap tables, admin keys and governance structures become the determinant of securities status — a direct diligence checklist for token investments.
insights.quote: It replaces a project’s unfalsifiable claim to be “sufficiently decentralized” with a statutory test based on control.
insights.locator: It settles the jurisdictional question

insights.claim: The bill would settle the SEC/CFTC jurisdictional boundary, which today is described as open to expansive and weaponizable interpretation.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Jurisdictional resolution removes a major discount applied to U.S. crypto business models; watch which agency captures spot market oversight for fee and registration flow.
insights.locator: It settles the jurisdictional question

insights.claim: CLARITY would impose issuer disclosure obligations, lockup periods and insider-trading restrictions on token issuers comparable to those already applied to public stocks, none of which currently exist.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Mandatory lockups and insider-selling limits would change token unlock dynamics and supply overhangs — a structural change to how token launches are underwritten.
insights.locator: As proposed, CLARITY contains unprecedented constraints

insights.claim: The charge that the legislation 'deregulates' crypto rests on the false premise that all crypto is already covered by securities laws, when courts have repeatedly said otherwise and it is not seriously disputed that assets like bitcoin and ethereum are not securities.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: The 'deregulation' framing is the main political obstacle; if it holds in the Senate, expect continued regulatory limbo rather than a stricter regime.
insights.quote: The Wild West that opponents fear is the thing we already have.
insights.locator: First, that CLARITY is “deregulation”

insights.claim: Objections that public officials holding crypto would benefit from the bill conflate government ethics with financial regulation, and an ethics regime written one asset class at a time invites whack-a-mole since self-dealers can route around it.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Identifies the likely poison-pill rider — an ethics amendment reaching only crypto assets is the specific mechanism that could sink or delay the bill.
insights.locator: Second, that officials who hold crypto

insights.claim: Voting the bill down does not constrain any official's holdings; it leaves those holdings unsupervised, so opponents describing an opaque, ruleless market are voting to preserve exactly that market.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: The inversion argument is the industry's core lobbying message — watch whether swing senators adopt it as cover for a yes vote.
insights.quote: Voting it down doesn’t constrain anyone’s holdings. Rather, it leaves them unsupervised.
insights.locator: As proposed, CLARITY contains unprecedented constraints

insights.claim: Bank warnings that stablecoin rewards would drain deposits are contradicted by a White House Council of Economic Advisers estimate putting the lending effect of a total ban at roughly $2.1 billion, about two hundredths of one percent of bank lending.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Quantifies the deposit-flight risk as immaterial, implying bank-sector opposition is competitive rather than prudential — a signal on how durable that lobbying block is.
insights.quote: This is an anti-competitive argument masquerading as a financial stability one.
insights.locator: Third, that stablecoin rewards will drain deposits

insights.claim: After months of negotiation, the bill text bars passive yield — any return economically or functionally equivalent to deposit interest — while preserving rewards tied to genuine activity, and the latest draft lets the Treasury Department add restrictions if deposit flight materializes.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Business models built on paying interest-like stablecoin yield are legislatively foreclosed; activity-linked rewards programs become the compliant design, with residual Treasury discretion as an ongoing risk.
insights.locator: That objection isn’t supported by evidence

themes.theme: Statute versus agency rulemaking: certainty as a product

insights.claim: Regulatory agencies cannot solve the problem alone because any commission rule lasts only until the next commission reverses it and can be tied up in court for years by anyone with standing.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Discount any crypto-friendly agency posture as temporary; only statutory outcomes should change long-duration capital allocation assumptions.
insights.quote: Any commission rule is a rule only until the next commission reverses it, and one that anyone with standing can tie up in court for years.
insights.locator: This isn’t a problem the regulatory agencies can solve

insights.claim: Institutions will not commit to investing in critical digital asset infrastructure while the legal framework may not survive the next election, making legal certainty itself the product being bought.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Implies a step-change in institutional capex into crypto rails conditional on passage — the trade is infrastructure and custody buildout, not just token beta.
insights.quote: Certainty is a product. Only a statute will deliver it.
insights.locator: Firms holding other people’s money should not have to build

insights.claim: An entire industry's legal treatment recently swung with a change of administration, demonstrating that enforcement-driven policy is not a stable foundation for compliance systems.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Political-cycle risk is the dominant variable in U.S. crypto business planning until a statute exists; size positions for reversal risk.
insights.locator: We just watched an entire industry’s legal treatment swing

themes.theme: Systemic scale has grown since FTX

insights.claim: The next failure will be bigger than FTX because crypto is no longer a retail market at the edge of the financial system.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Frames an unregulated large intermediary failure as a systemic tail risk rather than a contained retail event — relevant to counterparty exposure limits.
insights.quote: If the Senate doesn’t act now, the next failure will be bigger.
insights.locator: If the Senate doesn’t act now

insights.claim: Since the GENIUS Act passed in July 2025 and gave dollar-denominated stablecoins a federal framework, stablecoin supply has passed $300 billion, transaction volumes have risen sharply, and stablecoin issuers now sit among the largest holders of U.S. government debt.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuers as major Treasury buyers creates a two-way link between crypto flows and short-end rates — a macro channel worth monitoring.
insights.locator: Congress passed the GENIUS Act in July 2025

insights.claim: The GENIUS Act only set rules for the dollars moving onchain and left the blockchain rails they travel on entirely untouched, leaving a structural gap between regulated tokens and unregulated infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: The regulatory gap sits at the intermediary and rails layer — that is where the next accident and the next compliance spend both land.
insights.quote: But GENIUS only provides rules for the dollars moving onchain while leaving all the blockchain rails they travel on untouched.
insights.locator: Congress passed the GENIUS Act in July 2025

insights.claim: Tokenized assets have passed $30 billion in market value and are diversifying well beyond crypto-native products.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: A concrete size benchmark for the tokenization theme; growth beyond crypto-native collateral widens the addressable market for issuance and servicing platforms.
insights.locator: Everything else onchain has scaled too

insights.claim: The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation, whose depository subsidiary custodies more than $114 trillion of securities, processed its first production tokenized-asset transactions in July and launches its full tokenization service next month.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Core U.S. market plumbing going live on tokenization is the strongest single adoption datapoint here — it moves tokenization from pilot to default settlement infrastructure.
insights.locator: The Depository Trust and Clearing Corporation

insights.claim: BlackRock, Fidelity, Franklin Templeton and Goldman Sachs all run live digital asset businesses and have all publicly backed the market structure bill.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Traditional asset-manager support broadens the coalition beyond crypto-native lobbying and raises passage odds; these firms are also the likeliest beneficiaries of a statutory framework.
insights.locator: BlackRock, Fidelity, Franklin Templeton, and Goldman Sachs

insights.claim: The status quo is not a neutral state: the question is no longer whether digital asset markets will exist but what rules will govern them.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Useful mental model for reading any policy fight — inaction is itself a policy choice with a specific beneficiary, usually offshore and unregulated venues.
insights.quote: The question is no longer whether digital asset markets will exist. It is what rules will govern them.
insights.locator: Which means the status quo

insights.claim: Every week without a statutory rulebook is another week in which an exchange can hold Americans' assets without the safeguards they take for granted in every other market.
insights.speaker: Miles Jennings
insights.so_what: Establishes the industry's urgency framing; delay, not defeat, is the more likely outcome to hedge against.
insights.locator: Bipartisan negotiators in both chambers
